The Wall Street Journal reported that Micron is urging the Trump administration to block Apple's plan to source memory chips from Chinese suppliers. Details below.

Apple's China chip plan extends beyond the China market

Last month, just before Apple raised prices on several products due to ongoing memory shortages, Tim Cook told The Wall Street Journal that the US should reconsider its decision to restrict procurement from certain Chinese suppliers.

In the days that followed, The Wall Street Journal reported that Apple had been seeking Washington's approval to purchase chips from Chinese firm ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT). Meanwhile, the Financial Times reported that Apple was in talks with Yangtze Memory Technologies (YMTC) to procure chips. The Financial Times later reported that Apple was already testing DRAM chips from CXMT.

It's understood that CXMT and YMTC have both been listed by the US Department of Defense as Chinese military companies, while YMTC has also been placed on the Commerce Department's Entity List.

This move does not necessarily prohibit Apple from using their chips in products sold outside the US, but it has made any potential deal politically sensitive and has previously drawn opposition against the company.

Now, The Wall Street Journal reports that as Apple continues to lobby the Trump administration for approval to use Chinese memory chips in products sold outside the US—not limited to the China market alone—it faces opposition from Micron, which is lobbying officials to block the plan.

The report states:

According to people familiar with the matter, Apple CEO Tim Cook and other senior executives recently pitched a plan to Trump and officials including Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, proposing that Apple products sold outside the US use memory chips from Chinese firms CXMT and YMTC. Micron is the only US-based memory chipmaker of meaningful scale, and its CEO Sanjay Mehrotra and other senior executives have warned Lutnick and other government officials that allowing CXMT and other Chinese firms to sell chips to US tech companies—regardless of where the sales take place—could destroy the US domestic industry, much as China has played a role in destroying US steel and manufacturing.

In short, the overarching argument against Apple's plan is this: even if limited to the Chinese market, procuring memory from heavily state-subsidized Chinese suppliers could ultimately undermine US producers and weaken competition.

In addition, The Wall Street Journal reported that Micron said it could help ease the chip shortage by accelerating construction of domestic fabs and increasing US investment.

A few weeks ago, a Micron executive hinted that Apple's aggressive procurement practices had contributed to the memory shortage, telling The Wall Street Journal that "some of (its) customers" had been "very aggressive on pricing" during the 2023 market downturn. He added that these extremely low prices made the industry reluctant to invest in capacity expansion, sowing the seeds for today's supply tightness.

Returning to the report, The Wall Street Journal said the dispute between Apple and Micron has put the Trump administration in an awkward position, because "this lobbying battle is likely to force Trump to choose between two of his top economic priorities: lowering prices for American consumers and boosting domestic semiconductor production to reduce dependence on other countries."

Apple, for its part, has spent much of the past two years publicizing its investment commitments—such as its US$600 billion US manufacturing plan, its deal with Intel, and earlier a US$30 billion agreement with Broadcom.

These expenditures are widely seen as part of an effort to build relationships with the government, giving Apple political capital to offset controversial requests such as sourcing memory chips from restricted Chinese suppliers.

On the other side, Micron's market value has tracked the broader memory market. Its share price is up 191% year-to-date and a whopping 727% over the past 12 months, though volatility has increased recently. The stock is currently 23% below its late-June all-time high and fell 6.99% in a single day.

A White House spokesperson, responding to The Wall Street Journal, did not provide clear direction on how the administration plans to balance the competing priorities of Apple and Micron, saying only that it would work to "deliver investment and economic relief for the American people while protecting national security."

Do you think the Trump administration should approve Apple's procurement of components from CXMT and YMTC? Let us know in the comments.
